title-group.article-title: Fluorescence Guidance Reduces Operative Time for Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy in the Head and Neck

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: Prior studies have demonstrated the feasibility of fluorescently labeled tilmanocept for sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) in the oral cavity. We evaluated the added value of fluorescently-labeled tilmanocept in sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) of the oral cavity compared to gamma probe.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Healthy male New Zealand white rabbits received oral cavity injections of radioactive (Technetium 99m) and fluorescently (IRDye800) conjugated tilmanocept followed by either fluorescence guided (n=14) or gamma probe guided (n=14) SLNB performed 1 hour, 48 hours, or 5 days post-injection. Duration of the SLNB performed by two individuals was measured and compared using the two methods.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Fluorescence guidance resulted in a 1.8 fold reduction in time of SLN removal (median 104 seconds versus 191 seconds, p=0.05). For the fluorescence guided SLNB, 7.1% (1 of 14) had non-sentinel node tissue removed prior to the correct identification of the SLN, whereas gamma probe/radioactivity guided SLNB had 28.6% (4 of 14). When comparing operation time between attending and resident surgeon, time to identification of first SLN was not significantly different for fluorescence guided surgery (82 seconds vs 107 seconds, respectively) or with gamma probe (158 seconds vs 204 seconds); however, median times using the gamma probe were nearly double for both operators. We additionally show the durability of fluorescence signal up to 5 days and clear visualization of proposed tracer with commercially available intraoperative imagers.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The use of fluorescent labeled tilmanocept decreases operative time needed for SLNB as well as reduces the amount of non-sentinel tissue removed.

sec.title: Level of Evidence:
sec.p: 5, preclinical study

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is a surgical procedure to remove and examine the first echelon nodal basin, or sentinel lymph node(s) to which a primary tumor drains. Although the concept of SLNB was first introduced in 1951 during a total parotidectomy,1 it was not until nearly two decades later when this procedure became popularized by Cabanas et al.2 Currently SLNB is the standard of care for breast cancer, genitourinary cancers, and melanoma in patients with clinically negative lymph nodes and there is a growing body of evidence to support its use for treatment of early stage oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC).

Previously, for early stage clinical N0 OCSCC the standard management has been elective neck dissection; however, due to the fact that only about 20–30% of patients undergoing elective neck dissection will have positive nodal disease,3,4 SLNB was introduced as an alternative means to stage the neck. Two recent randomized controlled trials have shown similar oncologic outcomes including recurrence free survival, 3 year overall survival, and disease free survival in patients undergoing SLNB in conjunction with primary tumor resection compared to elective neck dissection.5,6 In addition, SLNB has been associated with decreased surgical morbidity, decreased hospital stay, and improved shoulder function and quality of life. Other studies have highlighted additional advantages of SLNB such as identifying aberrant sentinel nodes outside of the planned neck dissection field and reduced total cost.7–9 As a result, the NRG oncology group is currently enrolling patients in the United States into a multi-institutional randomized control trial aimed at definitively establishing the role of SLNB in this patient population.10

As SLNB in the head and neck becomes more widely accepted, there is a need for improved intraoperative tools to enhance visualization and accuracy of sentinel lymph node identification. Several studies have demonstrated the feasibility of using a single agent of radiolabeled (Technetium 99m) Tilmanocept conjugated to fluorescent IRDye800CW to provide radiotracer signal in addition to visual feedback in SLNB in bladder, prostate, endometrial cancer, rectal, and oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma in animal models.11–15 These studies, however, have primarily demonstrated feasibility, but have not provided direct comparisons with current standards of care. The purpose of this work was to directly compare fluorescent guided SLNB to radioactivity guided SLNB and illustrate the advantages of utilizing a single dual fluorescent and radioactive labeled agent in the operating room.

sec.title: Materials and Methods
sec.p: This non-survival animal study was approved by the UCSD Institution Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), protocol S17047. Dual labeled tilmanocept was prepared by covalently binding the fluorescent dye IRDye800CW (LI-COR Biosciences, Lincoln NE) to Tilmanocept (Navidea Biopharmaceuticals, Dublin OH) radiolabeled with either Gallium-68 or Technetium-99m as previously described.14 In this study, 28 healthy male New Zealand white rabbits received either buccal mucosa (n=12) or oral tongue (n=16) injections of dual labeled tilmanocept. Animals were randomly assigned to either gamma probe guided (n= 14) or fluorescent guided (n=14) cohorts and after injection, underwent SLNB performed after 1 hour (n=16), 48 hours (n=8), or 5 days (n=4) using the appropriate surgical adjunct. Prior to SLNB, each rabbit was euthanized by a lethal injection of sodium pentobarbital at 150mg/kg and neck fur was shaved and removed with Nair hair removal cream for optimal visualization. For fluorescent guided SLNB, either research grade Fluorobeam800 (Fluoptics, Grenoble, France) or clinical grade Rubina (Karl Storz, Tuttlingen, Germany) endoscopic camera system was used. Both fluorescent imaging systems were equipped with near infrared/ICG capabilities. For radioactivity guided SLNB, Neoprobe gamma detection system (Mammotome, Cincinnati, OH, USA) was used. All animal surgeries were performed by either a senior resident surgeon or attending surgeon and the time required for SLN removal was measured from first skin incision until confirmation of removal of the SLN ex vivo. Adjacent non-nodal tissue surrounding the SLN was then harvested in 4 separate pieces. The surgeon then confirmed the presence or absence of additional sentinel nodes using the assigned method for identification. Once confirmed that all sentinel nodes were removed with the primary identification method, this was verified with the second method of identification. After all SLNs were removed, bilateral neck dissections were performed in the cervical and submandibular regions and submandibular glands and primary injection site tissue (i.e. tongue or buccal mucosa) was obtained. Harvested SLN(s), adjacent non-nodal tissue surrounding SLN(s), non-sentinel lymph nodes, submandibular glands, and primary injection site were measured for weight, radioactivity, and fluorescence activity. Statistical comparison of medians was performed with Mann-Whitney U test. Notably two animal dissections were identified as outliers (dissection time greater than two times standard deviation above the mean), analysis with removal of outliers was also performed in parallel.

sec.title: Fluorescence guidance results in shorter time to sentinel lymph node identification
sec.p: SLNB was successfully performed in all 28 rabbits using either fluorescence guided (n=14) or gamma probe guided (n=14) techniques. The median time for identification of the first SLN was significantly shorter with fluorescence imaging (104 seconds) compared to the gamma probe (191 seconds), reducing operative time by 1.8 fold (p=0.05) (Figure 1). With removal of outliers, the median operative time was similarly reduced using fluorescence imaging (104 seconds vs 184 seconds, p=0.01). When stratifying operative times for SLNB performed after tongue injection, fluorescence guided SLNB also resulted in a reduction in time (105 seconds fluoro versus 211 seconds gamma, p=0.03 excluding outliers). However, this was not detected for rabbits undergoing buccal mucosal injections (84 seconds fluoro versus 114 seconds gamma). There was no difference between SLN biopsy dissection times by surgical method for rabbits with cervical sentinel lymph nodes (61%) detected compared to submandibular sentinel nodes (39%) (Table 1).

Multiple SLNs (2 to 4 per rabbit) were identified in eight animals. The average time to remove two SLNs was nearly twice as long when using gamma probe (392 seconds) compared to fluorescence (220 seconds). As only 8 rabbits harbored multiple sentinel nodes, statistical testing was not performed in this limited cohort. However, anecdotally removal of multiple lymph nodes was also faster using fluorescence guidance. For example, we identified 4 total SLNs (confirmed by fluorescence activity measurements following removal) in animal #408. Interestingly, it took only 390 seconds to complete removal of all 4 SLNs detected via fluorescence which was more than 3 minutes shorter than the time required to remove 2 SLNs using the gamma probe for animal #403 (total 595 seconds).

We observed that fluorescence guidance allowed for easier identification of the sentinel node for both resident and attending surgeon operators. Fluorescence guided and radioactivity guided SLNB times were not significantly different among individual operators; however, the median time for SLN identification and removal was nearly double using the gamma probe compared to fluorescence for both operators (resident surgeon median fluoro 107 seconds vs median gamma 204 seconds, attending surgeon median fluoro 83 seconds vs median gamma 158 seconds) potentially illustrating a more favorable learning curve using fluorescence visualization. With removal of outliers, the attending surgeon demonstrated significantly decreased operative times using fluorescence guidance (p=0.01).

sec.title: Fluorescence guided surgery reduced removal of non-sentinel node tissue
sec.p: During sentinel lymph node biopsy, often non-sentinel lymph node tissue may be removed before the sentinel node is ultimately identified. This can increase length of procedure and potentially increase morbidity if increased unnecessary dissection is performed. In this study, 7.1% (1 of 14 rabbits) of fluorescence guided procedures involved accidental removal of non-sentinel node tissue prior to the correct identification of the SLN. However, when using the gamma probe without fluorescence guidance, 28.6% (4 of 14 rabbits) had non-sentinel node tissue removed prior to correct SLN identification.

sec.title: Fluorescent tilmanocept can visualize sentinel lymph nodes for up to 5 days
sec.p: We previously demonstrated the longevity of both tilmanoscept and its fluorophore tag for up to 48 hours.14 In this study, we included evaluation of sentinel lymph node fluorescence at multiple time points: 12 animals received sentinel lymph node dissection 1 hour after injection, 8 animals received sentinel lymph node dissection 48 hours after injection. Additionally, 4 animals received sentinel lymph node dissection 5 days after injection, and only fluorescence aided surgery was performed in these animals as radioactivity was minimal at this point. The visualization of sentinel lymph nodes by fluorescence guidance was not impacted by the longer time between injection and dissection. (Figure 2) Time to sentinel lymph node identification did not significantly differ based on time between injection and procedure. The median time to sentinel node identification using fluorescence was 110 seconds when biopsy was performed 1 hour after injection, and 107 seconds after a 5 day delay between injection and procedure. Fluorescence signal persisted without decay after five days, showing a trend toward increased fluorescence signal at five days. The mean fluorescence within the tissue measuring 1435 intensity units (IU, SD 470.6) within the sentinel lymph node at 1 hour after injection and 2051 IU (SD 1280, p=0.097) at 5 days. Lastly, to demonstrate clinical feasibility of use for this agent, we also evaluated the visualization of fluorescence signal using existing ICG capable intraoperative technology (i.e. Karl Storz Rubina system) to simulate views that would be achievable in the operating room (Figure 3, images taken at 48 hours after injection).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Dual labeled tilmanocept (IRDye800CW-tilmanocept) with both fluorescence and radioactivity represents a promising new technology to improve the visualization of sentinel lymph nodes by providing visual feedback. We previously demonstrated that fluorescence guided sentinel lymph node biopsy is highly accurate in the head and neck14 as well as other disease sites,11,13,15 and in this study we demonstrate its ability to decrease operating time for sentinel lymph node identification by nearly half, compared to standard gamma probe. Furthermore, we demonstrate additional advantages of decreased removal of non-sentinel lymph node tissue, as well as longevity of fluorescence signal that can outlast radioactive signal (up to 5 days) and be retained in the sentinel node. Lastly, we demonstrate that this fluorescence signal can be clearly visualized with the currently available ICG capable intraoperative Storz Rubina camera.

Our study was powered to detect a difference between fluorescence based SLNB and gamma probe-based dissection, which showed a significant decrease in operative time with fluorescence guided surgery. Additional subgroup analyses were also evaluated, and some differences were also noted after outliers were removed. When results were stratified by primary injection site, operative times for animals undergoing tongue injection were also shortened when using fluorescence compared to radioactivity (gamma probe). This was felt to be due to the fact that fluorescence guided SLNB was superior in providing feedback on the depth of the SLN, facilitating dissection of deeper nodes associated with oral tongue lymphatic drainage. We noticed that lymphatic drainage after primary tongue injection tended to localize in the cervical region (94% of tongue tumors drained to cervical nodes) where lymph nodes were deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle rather than more superficial submandibular nodes which was the more common site of drainage following buccal injections (83% of buccal tumors drained to submandibular basin). Thus, the visual aid provided by fluorescence allowed for enhanced depth perception, however due to limited power we did not see a statistical difference between time to SLN identification in cervical nodes alone. Additional studies aimed at characterizing the relationship between depth of SLN and operating time could clarify the potential reasons behind these differences that we observed and highlight when fluorescence assistance might provide the most benefit.

In timed dissection of multiple sentinel lymph nodes, identification of a second and subsequent sentinel lymph nodes using fluorescence was faster than use of gamma probe. Multiple sentinel lymph nodes were found in 8 of 28 animals. When comparing mean operative times to identify the second SLN, it took an additional 116 seconds (range 166–316 seconds) for fluorescence guided and 222 seconds (range 162– 595 seconds) for gamma probe guided SLN biopsy. Although we were not powered to evaluate a statistical difference, the median time to second SLN identification was again double using gamma probe compared to fluorescence guided surgery. Similarly, for animals with greater than two sentinel lymph nodes, fluorescence guided surgery showed promising trends towards decreased length of surgery. Thus, in addition to fluorescence being helpful in reducing operative time for a single SLN, it may be even more beneficial in reducing total operative time when multiple SLNs are identified. Again, given limited animals that had multiple sentinel nodes, the study was likely underpowered to demonstrate statistical significance.

An additional benefit of using fluorescence for SLNB is that it can be visualized through the skin (Figure 3) for more superficial lymph nodes including contralateral nodes which were identified in 2 study animals. Clinically, visualization of the SLN prior to skin incision would be useful in guiding incision placement on the head and neck, especially if contralateral drainage is anticipated, and potentially allow for a smaller, less invasive incision which is particularly beneficial for patients concerned with the aesthetic appearance of their incision. Without visual feedback, it can commonly be difficult to visualize lymph nodes in certain areas of the head and neck such as the parotid region, and identification is often facilitated by adjunct imaging such as SPECT/CT.16 Although not the primary focus of the current study, we believe that application of our dual fluorescence and radioactive tracer would particularly be useful in providing visual and auditory intraoperative feedback during SLNB localizing to the parotid region, such as is common for cutaneous melanomas of the head and neck. These findings would need to be validated in patient procedures as compared to patients, the lymph node depth in animals is relatively superficial.

Another common clinical challenge in head and neck SLNB is removal of non-sentinel nodal tissue, particularly in complex anatomic regions. This can lead to prolonged operative and anesthesia times, as well as unnecessary surgical dissection. In our study, non-sentinel lymph node tissue was removed before sentinel lymph node identification in only 7% of cases using fluorescence guidance, compared to 29% with the traditional gamma probe. These preliminary findings suggest that dual-labeled tilmanocept may enhance surgical efficiency and precision by reducing the likelihood of unnecessary tissue removal during SLNB.

We also compared SLN biopsy times between an attending surgeon and senior resident surgeon. Although there was no significant difference between attending or resident operative times using fluorescence compared to gamma probe, the median time for SLN identification and removal was nearly double using the gamma probe compared to fluorescence for both operators (resident median fluorescence 107 seconds vs median gamma probe 204 seconds, attending median fluorescence 83 seconds vs median gamma probe 158 seconds) potentially illustrating a more favorable learning curve using fluorescence visualization.

Lastly, we performed SLNB at various time intervals following injection of dual labeled tilmanocept to assess the durability of the fluorescent signal. We found that fluorescence remained just as robust after our delayed five-day experiment and was clearly detectable using both research grade and currently available ICG capable intraoperative technology (i.e. Karl Storz Rubina system) (Figure 3) allowing potential easy translation to human studies given equipment that can already readily identify the IRDye800CW label.

The current gold standard for sentinel lymph node biopsy in oral cavity SCC includes injection of Tc-99m Tilmanocept (Lymphoseek) followed by lymphoscintigraphy with or without single-photon emission CT (SPECT) for multiplanar identification and localization of SLNs. With this method, imaging is typically performed 1–2 hours after injection with surgery within 24 hours.17 It is well accepted that technetium 99m although effective, has a short half-life (~6 hours). Additionally, the utility of this method requires the availability of nuclear imaging facilities and requires that the patient undergo surgery within 24–48 hours which is a major limitation. Although clinical studies and human trials are still needed, dual labeled tilmanocept can potentially overcome this limitation with the longevity of the fluorescent tracer that can outlast the radioactive gamma signal and last from 1 hour up to five days post injection, offering greater flexibility in scheduling SLNB.

For sentinel lymph node biopsy, many surgeons have used Tc-99m Tilmanocept along with blue dye visual tracers such as isosulfan blue dye (Lymphazurin) or methylene blue for intraoperative visualization as well as fluorescent tracers like ICG. In addition to staining at the injection site, the utility of blue dyes as an adjunct to support sentinel lymph node identification is limited by its quick passage through the sentinel node.18,19 Early studies demonstrated only about 60% of SLN visible by blue dye.18 Similar to IRDye800CW, fluorescent dyes such as ICG have also been used to improve visual feedback for SLN localization and demonstrated improved detection compared to blue dye.20 However, the usefulness of free ICG is still also limited by brief retention in sentinel nodes as well as potential decoupling from the radioactive tracer. Additionally, these optical tracers require a second injection performed intraoperatively. The longevity of a single injection fluorescent labeled tilmanoscept to both maintain fluorescence signal as well as remain bound within the sentinel node up to 5 days without flow through highlights another key advantage of the dual labeled agent, which are a concern in other models that have been reported in the literature such as ICG.21

Hybrid ICG Tc-99m nanocolloid and nanoscan tracers which allow non-covalent binging of ICG to the nanoparticle have recently been developed to promote retention of both radioactivity and fluorescence within nodal tissue; however, widespread use of nanocolloids is not universal.22,23 These dual tracer methods have shown feasibility in early pilot studies for early stage oral cavity cancer.24 Tilmanocept (Lymphoseek) is more widely utilized in the United States, supporting the development of IRDye800CW-tilmanocept. The inherent properties of IRDye800CW-tilmanocept features specific binding to mannose receptors (CD206) expressed on the surface of macrophages and dendritic cells as well as a covalently bound fluorescent label, thus radiotracer activity can be used for adjunct imaging to confirm sentinel node drainage and localize the nodal basin of interest, while fluorescence provides the intraoperative visual feedback without concern for flow through to non-sentinel nodes.14 Future studies would also involve direct comparison between Tilmanocept and nanocolloid based fluorescent compounds as well as IRDye800 versus ICG fluorescence signals to determine specific benefits and superiority of a single agent and single injection.

The present research is a limited proof of concept animal study clearly demonstrating the benefits of fluorescence in sentinel lymph node surgery. Limitations of our study include the small sample size as well as inherent limitations of using a rabbit model. This includes the relatively superficial depth of rabbit lymph nodes and size of the animal impacting operative times which may not directly extrapolate to human head and neck anatomy and dissection. Future human clinical trials and prospective studies with larger sample sizes are needed to fully investigate the clinical implications of this novel dual tracer and potential benefit of reduced intraoperative time, decreased non-sentinel node tissue removal, favorable learning curve as well as other advantages over current treatment modalities. Future work and next steps in our group are establishing early phase clinical trials for our dual labeled tracer for sentinel lymph node biopsy for multiple body sites, including the head and neck.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In conclusion, fluorescence-guided SLNB represents a promising advancement in head and neck oncology, offering enhanced efficiency, precision, and feasibility by providing visual feedback that reduces operating time and providing clear visualization using current ICG imaging technologies. Further clinical studies utilizing dual labeled tilmanocept can validate these findings and explore the potential integration of dual labeled fluorescence imaging into standard human SLNB protocols for the head and neck as well as other body sites.
